newsitem.title: GERMANY: German tax talks - start of cooperation or conflict?.
newsitem.headline: German tax talks - start of cooperation or conflict?.

text.p: Germany's government and opposition pushed off into uncharted waters on Monday, unsure whether their emergency tax reform talks will lead to a "grand coalition" or mark the start of a bitter 1998 election campaign.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl and Social Democrat (SPD) chairman Oskar Lafontaine have both firmly denied their rare "summit," meant as the first of several hastily-arranged sessions, would lead to a cabinet reshuffle to include the SPD.

But it aims at least for a "grand cooperation," some kind of all-party effort to fight the unemployment record of 4.7 million that overshadows all debates here and threatens to make Germany miss qualifying for Europe's single currency.
"Pull us out of the crisis!" Bild, Germany's largest daily, appealed in a bold headline. "Will we fall back into crisis or will we finally manage a turn for the better?"

The issues on the table are clear. Since the SPD majority in the upper house of parliament can block any new tax law, Kohl needs its support to cut taxes by 30 billion marks ($18 billion) and lower unit labour costs, thus promoting more jobs.
Public alarm over rising unemployment is now so fierce that the SPD cannot afford to stonewall. Voters in the October 1998 election would punish them for delaying a solution.
But the main opposition party cannot compromise so much that it ends up helping Kohl build a reelection campaign on the claim that he pulled Germany back from the brink.

The best-case scenario calls for agreement on laws this year to start cutting taxes in 1998. In the worst case, there will be no consensus and both parties will revert to confrontation to pin the blame for the failure on the other.
How the talks develop after the first meeting will also depend as much on leadership struggles within the two parties as on the economic challenges they face.

Recent opinion polls show Kohl's centre-right coalition trailing an opposition alliance of the SPD and Greens. The chancellor also does worse than either possible SPD challenger, Lafontaine or Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder.

Kohl, 66, hailed as "the eternal chancellor" last October when he became Bonn's longest-serving leader, has this year lost his legendary control over his Christian Democrats (CDU). The once-solid party is feuding on several fronts.

"Suddenly, Kohl is seen as the old man he is," the liberal Frankfurter Rundschau commented. "The psychology has changed. What that means for Bonn is not yet clear. Only the erosion of a 15-year regime is unavoidable."
Aides say Kohl would not be ready to share power with the SPD if the CDU concluded the reforms Bonn needed would be so unpopular that only a grand coalition could impose them.

But his loyal crown prince, parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble, would be open to the idea. He has said he would be "tempted" by the top job and seemed to be seeking common ground with Schroeder in a parliamentary debate last week.
Schaeuble, a tough leader confined to a wheelchair since a failed assassination attempt in 1990, also comes out at the top of surveys on Germany's most popular politicians.
That leads to the SPD's leadership problem. Lafontaine, the feisty Saar state premier who already failed in 1990 to unseat Kohl, is the party's presumed but not yet confirmed candidate for next year.
But Schroeder outscores him in popularity polls and ranks as a far more likely ally for Schaeuble than the party leader.
"The SPD is in a dilemma," said Hamburg political scientist Joachim Raschke. "It has to balance off goals, coalition prospects and people. It all has to fit, but with whom?"
Although Schroeder is the SPD's economic policy spokesman and is known to criticise party decisions, he was not made part of the delegation to meet Kohl.
That could come back to haunt Lafontaine if he gives in too much for the taste of the left-leaning party's rank and file.
Schroeder has already started canvassing support for an unconventional line in 1998 including some Euroscepticism.
